Myocardial infarction (Ml) involving the left ventricle (LV) commonly leads to scarring and a sustained
reduction in contractile function; however, contractile function of the right ventricle (RV) almost always
returns to normal following MI. Some of the reasons for protection of the RV from infarction include:
« The relatively small muscle mass and afterload of the RV create less oxygen demand and
necessitate lower oxygen extraction at rest. This allows for a large capacity to increase oxygen
extraction during periods of ischemia.
* The relatively low systolic pressure of the RV (eg, <25 mm Hg) allows for coronary perfusion
throughout the cardiac cycle; during MI, this enables the RV to pull blood flow from collateral vessels
during both systole and diastole. In contrast, the high systolic pressure of the LV (eg, 120 mm Hg)
blocks coronary blood flow of the LV walls during systole, allowing for perfusion during diastole only.

These factors likely contribute to the typical clinical course of MI involving the RV, which is acute RV
contractile dysfunction often leading to profound hypotension and hemodynamic instability; acute mortality
risk is high, but there is minimal long-term RV dysfunction for those who survive.
educationalObjective:
The right ventricle (RV) is relatively protected from myocardial infarction (MI), and contractile function of the
RV usually returns to normal following MI. Factors contributing to this protection include relatively small
muscle mass with high capacity to increase oxygen extraction, perfusion throughout the cardiac cycle, and
heightened ischemic preconditioning.

A 1-hour-old girl is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to respiratory failure. The patient was
born at 41 weeks gestation via emergency cesarean delivery due to prolonged fetal bradycardia during
labor. Membranes were ruptured at delivery, and thick meconium was present. Respiratory rate was
80/min, and pulse oximetry showed an oxygen saturation of 88% in the right hand; examination revealed
grunting and retractions. The patient was intubated and ventilated in the delivery room. Echocardiogram
shows a structurally normal heart with increased pulmonary artery pressure and right-to-left blood flow
through a patent foramen ovale. A medication with which of the following mechanisms of action is most
appropriate for this patient?

options.A: \|ncreased cyclic AMP in bronchial smooth muscle cells
options.B: Increased cyclic GMP in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells
options.C: Inhibition of Na-K-ATPase in cardiac myocytes
options.D: Inhibition of phospholipase A2 enzyme activity
options.E: Reduced surface tension at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli

explanations.A:
(Choice A) Albuterol stimulates adenylyl cyclase and increases cyclic AMP within airway smooth muscle
cells. This mechanism results in relaxation and dilation of airways (ie, bronchodilation), not of vasculature
(ie, vasodilation), and therefore does not decrease PVR.
explanations.C:
(Choice C) Na-K-ATPase inhibition by digoxin ultimately increases intracellular calcium concentration.
This results in increased myocyte contractile performance and improved ventricular systolic function in
patients with systolic heart failure (low ejection fraction). This neonate has no problems with ventricular
contractility and therefore digoxin would not be helpful.
explanations.D:
(Choice D) Corticosteroids bind to intracellular glucocorticoid receptors and alter gene transcription,
causing decreased expression of phospholipase A2. This leads to decreased release of arachidonic acid
and its inflammatory metabolites. This mechanism would not significantly alter PVR in the setting of PPHN.
explanations.E:
(Choice E) Surfactant therapy reduces surface tension at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli and treats
respiratory distress syndrome, a condition that can cause elevated pulmonary artery pressures but is seen
nearly exclusively in premature neonates. This patient's gestational age makes this diagnosis extremely
unlikely.

This neonate has elevated pulmonary artery pressure with consequent right-to-left shunting of blood
through fetal circulatory pathways (eg, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus), findings which are consistent with
persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).
In general, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is physiologically elevated in the fetus. During the initial
breaths after birth, alveolar oxygen concentration increases, resulting in pulmonary artery vasodilation and
a rapid reduction of PVR. PPHN is caused by failure of PVR to decrease, leading to decreased
pulmonary blood flow and alveolar gas exchange. Common causes of PPHN are lung hypoplasia (eg,
congenital diaphragmatic hernia) and meconium aspiration syndrome (likely in this patient with thick
meconium and grunting/retractions).
Treatment of PPHN is aimed at decreasing PVR and includes supplemental oxygen (acts as a pulmonary
vasodilator) and inhaled nitric oxide, a potent vasodilator that acts on guanylate cyclase to increase
cyclic GMP (cGMP) in the smooth muscle cells of the pulmonary arteries. Increased cGMP results in

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn is caused by failure of pulmonary vascular resistance

An autopsy is performed on a 45-year-old man found dead at home. Cardiac examination reveals
calcification of the mitral annulus that is mostly confined to the posterior annulus with limited extension to
the leaflet tissue. There are no calcium deposits on the base of the anterior mitral leaflet or the mitral
commissures. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with these pathologic findings?

explanations.E:
(Choice E).

Unlike rheumatic mitral disease, which often causes significant mitral stenosis, MAC only rarely causes
mitral stenosis and is usually hemodynamically insignificant. However, the presence of MAC (eg, detected
via echocardiography) may be a marker for extensive coronary artery disease.
explanations.B:
(Choice B) Dilated cardiomyopathy can involve enlargement of the mitral valve annulus (often leading to
secondary mitral regurgitation), but it is not known to significantly contribute to mitral valve calcification.
explanations.C:
(Choice C) Infective endocarditis involves valvular vegetation consisting of platelets, fibrin, bacterial or
fungal microorganisms, and inflammatory cells (eg, neutrophils, macrophages). Calcification is not typical.
explanations.D:
(Choice D) Myxomatous valve degeneration can lead to mitral valve prolapse. MAC may be somewhat
encouraged by mitral valve prolapse (due to annular microinjury caused by high leaflet tension), but CKD
has a much stronger association.

The autopsy finding of calcification primarily affecting the posterior mitral annulus is consistent with age-
related mitral annular calcification (MAC), a process that is accelerated by chronic kidney disease
(CKD).
The pathophysiology of MAC is believed to be similar to that of both atherosclerosis and age-related calcific
aortic valve disease. Endothelial injury and subsequent dysfunction allow for subendothelial lipid
deposition, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and eventual fibroblast differentiation into osteoblast-like cells
that facilitate calcium deposition. CKD, which causes impaired phosphate clearance and disordered
calcium balance (eg, secondary hyperparathyroidism), results in an elevated calcium-phosphorus product
(the total amount of calcium and phosphorus circulating in the blood) that likely accelerates the calcium
deposition process.
Primary involvement of the posterior mitral annulus with sparing of the anterior annulus and valve
leaflets (C-shaped pattern) is characteristic of age-related MAC, perhaps owing to relatively high
hemodynamic pressure or stress exerted on the endothelium at the base of the posterior leaflet. This
deposition pattern is in contrast with rheumatic mitral valve disease, which is driven by immunologic cross-
reactivity between streptococcal and valve leaflet antigens, and involves calcification primarily affecting the
valve commissures with lesser involvement of any part of the annulus
educationalObjective:
Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is an age-related process with pathophysiology similar to atherosclerosis;
the process is accelerated by chronic kidney disease. MAC characteristically involves calcification primarily
affecting the posterior annulus with sparing of the anterior annulus and valve leaflets (C-shaped pattern).
